$$
S=\{x\in {{field-1}}\,:\,x>{{field-2}}\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The set $S$ contains all integers greater than $-4,$ including $-4.$

In other words, $S$ contains all integers greater than $-5,$ *excluding* $-5.$ 

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S=\{x\in Z\,:\,x>-5\}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\ge -4.$ This gives

$$
S=\{x\in Z\,:\,x\ge -4\}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186196462 :answer-field/correct 17592186196464 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186196458 :answer-field/correct 17592186196460 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186287849 :question/problem "Find the missing coefficients in the conditional definition of the set $\{-\frac{1}{2},3\}$ given below.

$\{-\frac{1}{2},3\}=\{q\in Q\,:\,4{q}^{2}\,-$
{{field-1}}
$q\,-$
{{field-2}}
$=0\}$" :question/worked-solution "The given set contains the roots $q\in Q$ of some quadratic polynomial $p(q).$

Since the quadratic polynomial has roots ${q}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}$ and ${q}_{2}=3,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=4,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(q) & =a(q-{q}_{1})(q-{q}_{2}) \\  & =4\cdot (q-(-\frac{1}{2}))(q-3) \\  & =4(q+\frac{1}{2})(q-3) \\  & =4({q}^{2}-\frac{5q}{2}-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =4{q}^{2}-10q-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
\{-\frac{1}{2},3\}=\{q\in Q\,:\,4{q}^{2}-10q-6=0\}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186287853 :question/problem "Find the missing coefficients in the conditional definition of the set $\{1\pm \text{i}\}$ given below.

$\{1\pm \text{i}\}=\{z\in C\,:\,2{z}^{2}\,-$
{{field-1}}
$z\,+$

$=0\}$" :question/worked-solution "The given set contains the roots $z\in C$ of some quadratic polynomial $p(z).$

Since the quadratic polynomial has roots ${z}_{1}=1-\text{i}$ and ${z}_{2}=1+\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=2,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =a(z-{z}_{1})(z-{z}_{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (z-(1-\text{i}))(z-(1+\text{i})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(1-\text{i})z-(1+\text{i})z+(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(1-\text{i}+1+\text{i})z+((1)^{2}-(\text{i})^{2})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(2)z+(1+1)) \\  & =2{z}^{2}-4z+4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
\{1\pm \text{i}\}=\{z\in C\,:\,2{z}^{2}-4z+4=0\}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198873 :question/problem "Describe the set $S=\{-5,-10,-20,-40,...\}$ using a constructive definition.

$$
S=\{{{field-1}}\,:\,n\in {{field-2}}\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the elements of our set

$$
-5,\,-10,\,-20,\,-40,\,…
$$

form an infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{-10}{-5} \\  & =\frac{-20}{-10} \\  & =\frac{-40}{-20} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in N,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =(-5)\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =(-5)\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot {2}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S=\{-\frac{5}{2}\cdot {2}^{n}\,:\,n\in N\}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186196500 :answer-field/correct "answer-1992cc29-bfe9-5821-ab65-85db7c9275d1" :answer-field/choices ["answer-cde8a085-4109-5cb9-b7e6-882a1aca743e" "answer-fbe45b33-5883-51ed-9f7c-2fa52c2e29d6" "answer-288cc4b2-c914-5214-82ea-49b388ebac4a" "answer-1992cc29-bfe9-5821-ab65-85db7c9275d1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cde8a085-4109-5cb9-b7e6-882a1aca743e" :answer/id #uuid "cde8a085-4109-5cb9-b7e6-882a1aca743e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-5\cdot {2}^{n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fbe45b33-5883-51ed-9f7c-2fa52c2e29d6" :answer/id #uuid "fbe45b33-5883-51ed-9f7c-2fa52c2e29d6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {5}^{n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-288cc4b2-c914-5214-82ea-49b388ebac4a" :answer/id #uuid "288cc4b2-c914-5214-82ea-49b388ebac4a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{5}\cdot {2}^{n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1992cc29-bfe9-5821-ab65-85db7c9275d1" :answer/id #uuid "1992cc29-bfe9-5821-ab65-85db7c9275d1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{5}{2}\cdot {2}^{n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186196496 :answer-field/correct 17592186196499 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186287864 :question/problem "Describe the set $S=\{2,1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4},...\}$ using a constructive definition.

$$
S=\{{{field-1}}\,:\,n\in {{field-2}}\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the elements of our set

$$
2,\,1,\,\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{4},\,…
$$

form an infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{1} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in N,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{-1} \\  & =4\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S=\{4\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}\,:\,n\in N\}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "activity-55d163d3-8f28-5869-a65b-cfaaab7569eb" :activity/id #uuid "55d163d3-8f28-5869-a65b-cfaaab7569eb" :activity/title "Describing Sets Using Set-Builder Notation" :activity/type :activity.type/review :activity/scope 17592186049076 :activity/course 17592186046658 :activity/steps ["step-43789ff6-ead3-53a4-9c70-d7e0bdd62fe0" "step-b48819c1-8133-563a-afd7-f37f211bbce6" "step-e3ae9ce9-3f42-51dc-87d2-39964c93e221" "step-3a19ba88-b779-5826-958c-8abfa367305b" "step-e1124dcc-a673-55f5-863e-080064a239ce"] :activity/first-step "step-43789ff6-ead3-53a4-9c70-d7e0bdd62fe0" :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id "step-43789ff6-ead3-53a4-9c70-d7e0bdd62fe0" :step/id #uuid "43789ff6-ead3-53a4-9c70-d7e0bdd62fe0" :step/content 17592186198868 :step/next "step-b48819c1-8133-563a-afd7-f37f211bbce6" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-b48819c1-8133-563a-afd7-f37f211bbce6" :step/id #uuid "b48819c1-8133-563a-afd7-f37f211bbce6" :step/content 17592186287849 :step/next "step-e3ae9ce9-3f42-51dc-87d2-39964c93e221" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-e3ae9ce9-3f42-51dc-87d2-39964c93e221" :step/id #uuid "e3ae9ce9-3f42-51dc-87d2-39964c93e221" :step/content 17592186287853 :step/next "step-3a19ba88-b779-5826-958c-8abfa367305b" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-3a19ba88-b779-5826-958c-8abfa367305b" :step/id #uuid "3a19ba88-b779-5826-958c-8abfa367305b" :step/content 17592186198873 :step/next "step-e1124dcc-a673-55f5-863e-080064a239ce" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id "step-e1124dcc-a673-55f5-863e-080064a239ce" :step/id #uuid "e1124dcc-a673-55f5-863e-080064a239ce" :step/content 17592186287864 :db/ensure [:step/validate]}]

set as follows:\n\n$$\n{1\\pm \\text{i}}={z\\in C\\,:\\,2{z}^{2}-4z+4=0}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186287857 :question/id #uuid "250dc34e-ac8d-50ac-8f72-1123fa8a7b34" :question/math-academy-id "q-183751" & =3(x+3)({x}^{2}-\\sqrt{5}x+\\sqrt{5}x-(\\sqrt{5})^{2}) \\\\  & =3(x+3)({x}^{2}-5) \\\\  & =3({x}^{3}-5x+3{x}^{2}-15) \\\\  & =3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-45\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can express [{:db/id 17592186199425 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199577 :tutorial/content "As previously seen, we can define sets using so-called *constructive definitions* of the form\n\n$$\n\\big\\{ {\\color{blue}\\textrm{rule}} \\: : \\: {\\color{blue}\\textrm{base set}} \\big\\}\n$$\n\n \n\nwhere the ${\\color{blue}\\textrm{rule}}$ is an expression (or formula) that depends on a variable that *constructs* elements of our set when the variable runs over some ${\\color{blue}\\textrm{base set}}.$ \n\nFor example, the set $A,$ given by\n\n$$\nA = \\big\\{ 2n+1\\, : \\, n\\in\\mathbb N_0 \\big \\}\n$$\n\nis defined constructively and contains all positive odd numbers:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A & ={2n+1\\,:\\,n\\in {N}_{0}} \\\\  & ={2(0)+1,\\,2(1)+1,\\,2(2)+1,\\,2(3)+1,\\,…} \\\\  & ={1,3,5,7,…}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nSometimes, it's helpful to write a set using a constructive definition. For example, how might we express the following set constructively?\n\n$$\nB = \\big\\{ 4, 7, 10, 13, \\ldots \\big\\}\n$$\n\nFirst, notice that the elements of our set \n\n$$\n4,\\quad 7,\\quad 10,\\quad 13,\\quad \\ldots\n$$\n\nform an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=3{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}d & =3 \\\\  & =7-4 \\\\  & =10-7 \\\\  & =13-10 \\\\  & ⋮\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the $n$th term $a_n$ of our sequence for $n\\in\\mathbb N$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\\cdot d \\\\  & =4+(n-1)\\cdot 3 \\\\  & =4+3n-3 \\\\  & =3n+1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can define our set constructively as follows:\n\n$$\nB = \\big\\{ 3n+1 \\: : \\: n \\in \\mathbb{N} \\big\\}\n$$\n\nThe expression $3n+1$ generates the elements of our set when $n$ runs over $\\mathbb{N}.$ \n\nNote the following:\n\n- A bar \"$\\mid$\" is just as acceptable as a colon to separate the rule from the base set. 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145
